chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
title: Charlie Holmes, Duke Ellington and lip trouble
summary: Charlie Holmes would not join Ellington after Hodges left; Dance and Caldwell talk about his refusing to record and lip problems.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Uh-huh. And so when Johnny left Duke and went for himself, we used to ask Charlie -- he was working with Luis, and said, Charlie, why don't you go on in to Duke, (unintelligible) to get Charlie. And because Charlie played a whole lot like Johnny.

You know. (Unintelligible) hear what Charlie would do. And Charlie wouldn't take it. I asked Charlie about it here about three years ago, said, no, Happy (unintelligible), we made those recordings with Clyde Bernhardt in '72. He says, no. I says, well, Charlie, why? He said, I think on account of him and Johnny was from the same --

Well, you know, I've heard a story with him, oh, two years before those records with Bernhardt. and he said he didn't like recording, and he wasn't going to record any more. And then when I heard them, he didn't sound too bad. But I -- you know, I think the lip muscles are -- you really got to work at it a little bit to --
Well, that can happen to some saxophone players, you know. I know some fellows that had lip trouble. One guy had lip trouble. His lips, the muscles of his lips became something like paralyzed.
I mean that's almost like, (unintelligible), but you really got to play to keep those muscles up.
That's right, what you have to do.
But Charlie, I mean, you know, I guess he's (unintelligible). I don't know.
